title: Softmax and scaled dot-product attention
summary: Softmax exponentiates and normalises, so only differences between scores matter; subtracting the maximum first prevents overflow. Dot products of d_k-wide random vectors have a spread of about √d_k, which saturates softmax, so scores are divided by √d_k. A causal mask adds −∞ above the diagonal so each token attends only to itself and earlier tokens: softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k + M) V.
llm_link: This is the exact attention formula inside GPT-style models. The causal mask is what lets a model train on every next-token prediction in a passage in one parallel pass, and it is also why, during generation, a token never changes once it has been produced.
key_ideas: softmax(s + c) = softmax(s): only differences matter, so subtract max(s) for numerical safety.
Multiplying scores by a large number makes softmax nearly one-hot; shrinking them makes it nearly uniform.
q · k with d_k random unit-variance entries has a standard deviation of about √d_k; dividing by √d_k brings it back to about 1.
Causal mask: −∞ above the diagonal before softmax gives exactly zero weight to future tokens; rows still sum to 1.
Five steps: Q Kᵀ, ÷ √d_k, + mask, softmax each row, × V.

options: It overflows and has no answer
quiz.explain: Only the difference matters: it equals softmax([1, 0]) = [e/(e+1), 1/(e+1)] ≈ [0.73, 0.27]. A naive implementation overflows, which is why we subtract the maximum first.

quiz.q: q and k have 256 entries each, all random with variance 1. Roughly how large is a typical q · k?
quiz.explain: The variance of a sum of 256 independent unit-variance products is 256, so the standard deviation is √256 = 16. Dividing by √d_k = 16 brings it back to about 1.

quiz.q: Why is a saturated (nearly one-hot) softmax bad at the start of training?
options: Its gradient is almost zero, so the attention weights barely learn
It makes the rows sum to more than 1
quiz.explain: When one weight is close to 1 and the rest close to 0, small changes to the scores barely change the output, so very little gradient flows back to W_Q and W_K.

quiz.q: With a causal mask on a 4-token sequence, how many nonzero weights does the third row of A have?
quiz.explain: Token 3 may attend to tokens 1, 2 and itself. The fourth entry is masked to −∞ before softmax and becomes exactly 0.

quiz.q: Why does a GPT need the causal mask during training?
options: Because every position is trained to predict the next token in parallel, and it must not see that token
To stop the model attending to padding
Because softmax cannot handle long sequences
quiz.explain: All T next-token predictions are made in one pass. Without the mask, position t could simply copy token t + 1 from the input instead of predicting it.

tests.name: no overflow for large scores
tests.code:

out=softmax(np.array([1000.0,1001.0,999.0]))
assert np.all(np.isfinite(out)), f'got {out}: np.exp(1000) overflows to inf. Subtract the maximum first.'

tests.name: works on each row of a table
tests.code:

assert out.shape==(2,3), f'shape should be unchanged, got {out.shape}'
assert np.allclose(out.sum(axis=1),1), f'each row should sum to 1, got {out.sum(axis=1)}. Did you use keepdims=True and the right axis?'

problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def score_spread(d_k, n=20000, seed=0, scaled=False):
    """Standard deviation of q . k for n random pairs of vectors whose entries are standard normal.
    If scaled is True, divide each score by sqrt(d_k) first."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    q = rng.normal(size=(n, d_k))
    k = rng.normal(size=(n, d_k))
    scores = (q * k).sum(axis=1)
    if scaled:
        scores = scores / np.sqrt(d_k)
    return np.std(scores)

# Once it works, predict and then print: score_spread(1), score_spread(16), score_spread(64), score_spread(64, scaled=True)

problems.title: Causal scaled attention (GPT, step 4)
problems.prompt:
Turn last lesson's attention head into the real thing. Your stable softmax and the GPT so far are in the starter.

  1. causal_mask(T): a (T, T) array with 0 on and below the diagonal and -np.inf above it.
  2. causal_attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv): returns (out, A) with A = softmax(Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k) + mask) on each row and out = A @ V.

Careful: 0 * -np.inf is nan, so do not build the mask by multiplying. np.triu(..., k=1) keeps the part strictly above the diagonal and puts zeros elsewhere.

import numpy as np
def _ref(X,Wq,Wk,Wv):
    Q,K,V=X@Wq,X@Wk,X@Wv
    T=len(X)
    S=Q@K.T/np.sqrt(Q.shape[1])
    S=np.where(np.tril(np.ones((T,T)))==1,S,-np.inf)

ro,rA=_ref(X,Wq,Wk,Wv)

problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    shifted = x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)   # largest entry becomes 0: no overflow
    e = np.exp(shifted)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

# ---- the character-level GPT so far (lessons 9.1 to 9.5) ----
text = "hello world"
vocab = sorted(set(text))
stoi = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(vocab)}
def encode(s):
    return [stoi[ch] for ch in s]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, d_k = 8, 4
E = rng.normal(size=(len(vocab), d))           # embedding table (V, d)
X = E[np.array(encode("hello"))]               # (T, d) = (5, 8)
Wq = rng.normal(size=(d, d_k))
Wk = rng.normal(size=(d, d_k))
Wv = rng.normal(size=(d, d_k))

# ---- step 4: scaled, causal attention (this lesson) ----
def causal_mask(T):
    """(T, T) array: 0 on and below the diagonal, -inf above it."""
    return np.triu(np.full((T, T), -np.inf), k=1)

def causal_attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv):
    """Returns (out, A) with A = softmax(Q Kᵀ / sqrt(d_k) + mask) and out = A V."""
    Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
    T, dk = Q.shape
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(dk) + causal_mask(T)
    A = softmax(S, axis=-1)
    return A @ V, A
